paragraphs: “Go on,” he said. “Tell me what happened that night.”

“What more is there to tell? I was lying there, and I thought I heard the master shout. Before that, Grigory Vassilyevitch had suddenly got up and come out, and all at once he gave a scream, and then everything went silent and dark. I lay there waiting with my heart pounding. I couldn’t stand it. At last I got up and went out. I saw the window on the left standing open to the garden. I stepped over to the left to listen whether he was sitting there alive, and I heard the master moving about and sighing, so I knew he was alive. ‘Ech!’ I thought. I went to the window and called to the master, ‘It’s me.’ And he called back to me, ‘He’s been here, he’s been here; he’s run away.’ He meant Dmitri Fyodorovitch had been. ‘He’s killed Grigory!’ ‘Where?’ I whispered. ‘There, in the corner,’ he said, pointing. He was whispering too. ‘Wait a bit,’ I said. I went to the corner of the garden to look, and there I found Grigory Vassilyevitch lying by the wall, covered in blood, unconscious. So it’s true, I thought, Dmitri Fyodorovitch has been here. And right then I made up my mind to finish it, because Grigory Vassilyevitch, even if he was alive, would see nothing of it, lying there senseless. The only danger was that Marfa Ignatyevna might wake up. I felt that at the time, but the longing to get it done came over me so strongly that I could hardly breathe. I went back to the window and said to the master, ‘She’s here, she’s come; Agrafena Alexandrovna has come, she wants to be let in.’ And he started like a baby. ‘Where is she?’ he gasped, but he couldn’t believe it. ‘She’s standing there,’ I said. ‘Open up.’ He looked out of the window at me, half believing and half distrusting, but afraid to open. ‘Why, he’s afraid of me now,’ I thought. And it was funny. It came to me to knock on the window frame, in front of him, before his eyes, those taps we’d agreed on as the signal that Grushenka had come. He didn’t seem to believe my word, but as soon as he heard the taps, he ran straight to open the door. He opened it. I would have gone in, but he stood in the way to stop me getting past. ‘Where is she? Where is she?’ He looked at me, trembling all over. ‘Well,’ I thought, ‘if he’s as frightened of me as all that, it looks bad!’ And my legs went weak with fear that he wouldn’t let me in, or would cry out, or Marfa Ignatyevna would come running, or something else would happen. I don’t remember now, but I must have stood there pale, facing him. I whispered to him, ‘Why, she’s there, right there under the window; how is it you don’t see her?’ ‘Bring her, then, bring her.’ ‘She’s afraid,’ I said; ‘the noise frightened her, she’s hiding in the bushes; go and call to her yourself from the study.’ He ran to the window and set the candle in it. ‘Grushenka,’ he called, ‘Grushenka, are you there?’ Though he called that, he wouldn’t lean out of the window, he wouldn’t move away from me, because he was panic-stricken; he was so scared he didn’t dare turn his back on me. ‘Why, there she is,’ I said. I went up to the window and leaned right out of it. ‘There she is; she’s in the bush, laughing at you, can’t you see her?’ He believed it all at once. He was shaking all over—he was terribly crazy about her—and he leaned right out of the window. I snatched up that iron paperweight from his table; do you remember it, the one weighing about three pounds? I swung it and hit him on the top of the skull with the corner of it. He didn’t even cry out. He just sank down suddenly, and I hit him again, and a third time. And on the third blow I knew I’d broken his skull. He suddenly rolled onto his back, face up, covered in blood. I looked myself over. There was no blood on me, not a spot. I wiped the paperweight and put it back. I went up to the ikons, took the money out of the envelope, and threw the envelope on the floor, with the pink ribbon beside it. I went out into the garden, trembling all over, straight to the apple tree with the hollow in it—you know that hollow. I’d marked it long before and put a rag and a piece of paper ready in it. I wrapped all the notes in the rag and pushed it deep down into the hole. And there it stayed for more than two weeks. I took it out later, when I came out of the hospital. I went back to my bed, lay down, and thought, ‘If Grigory Vassilyevitch has been killed outright, it may go badly for me, but if he’s not killed and he recovers, it’ll be first-rate, because then he’ll testify that Dmitri Fyodorovitch was here, and so he must have killed him and taken the money.’ Then I began groaning, from suspense and impatience, so as to wake Marfa Ignatyevna as soon as possible. At last she got up and rushed to me, but when she saw Grigory Vassilyevitch wasn’t there, she ran out, and I heard her scream in the garden. And that set it all going and put my mind at rest.”

He stopped. Ivan had listened the whole time in dead silence, without stirring or taking his eyes off him. As he told his story, Smerdyakov glanced at him now and then, but mostly kept his eyes turned away. When he finished, he was clearly agitated and was breathing hard. Sweat stood out on his face. But there was no telling whether it was remorse he felt, or something else.
“Wait,” cried Ivan, thinking it over. “What about the door? If he only opened the door to you, how could Grigory have seen it open earlier? Grigory saw it open before you went in.”

It was remarkable that Ivan spoke quite amiably, in a different tone, not angry as before. If anyone had opened the door at that moment and looked in at them, he would surely have concluded that they were talking peacefully about some ordinary, if interesting, subject.

“As for that door, and Grigory Vassilyevitch having seen it open, that’s just his imagination,” said Smerdyakov with a wry smile. “He’s not a man, I assure you, he’s an obstinate mule. He didn’t see it, he only fancied he had, and there’s no shaking him. It’s our good luck he took that notion into his head, because after that they can’t fail to convict Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

“Listen ...” said Ivan, seeming bewildered again and straining to grasp something. “Listen. There are a lot of questions I want to ask you, but I forget them ... I keep forgetting and getting muddled. Yes. Tell me this at least. Why did you open the envelope and leave it there on the floor? Why didn’t you simply carry off the envelope?... When you were telling me, you spoke of it as if it were the right thing to do ... but why, I can’t understand....”

“I did that for a good reason. Suppose a man knew all about it, as I did, for instance. Suppose he’d seen those notes before, and maybe had put them in that envelope himself, and had seen the envelope sealed and addressed with his own eyes. If such a man had done the murder, what would make him tear open the envelope afterwards, especially in such desperate haste, when he’d know for certain the notes must be inside it? No, if the robber had been someone like me, he’d simply have put the envelope straight in his pocket and got away with it as fast as he could. But it would be quite different with Dmitri Fyodorovitch. He only knew about the envelope by hearsay; he’d never seen it. If he’d found it, say, under the mattress, he’d have torn it open as quickly as possible to make sure the notes were in it. And he’d have thrown the envelope down without having time to think that it would be evidence against him. Because he wasn’t a habitual thief and had never actually stolen anything before, since he’s a gentleman born. And if he did bring himself to steal, it wouldn’t be real stealing, just taking what was his own, because he’d told the whole town beforehand that he meant to, and had even bragged out loud in front of everyone that he’d go and take his property from Fyodor Pavlovitch. I didn’t say that openly to the prosecutor when I was examined. Quite the contrary, I led him to it with a hint, as though I didn’t see it myself, and as though he’d thought of it on his own and I hadn’t prompted him; so that Mr. Prosecutor’s mouth positively watered at my suggestion.”
“But can you really have thought of all that on the spot?” cried Ivan, overcome with astonishment. He looked at Smerdyakov again with alarm.
“Goodness me! Could anyone think of all that in such a desperate hurry? It was all thought out beforehand.”
“Well ... well, it was the devil who helped you!” Ivan cried again. “No, you’re not a fool, you’re far cleverer than I thought....”

He got up, clearly meaning to walk across the room. He was in terrible distress. But the table blocked his way, and there was hardly room to pass between the table and the wall, so he only turned round where he stood and sat down again. Perhaps being unable to move irritated him, because he suddenly cried out almost as furiously as before.

“Listen, you miserable, contemptible creature! Don’t you understand that the only reason I haven’t killed you is that I’m keeping you to answer for it tomorrow at the trial? God sees,” Ivan raised his hand, “perhaps I too was guilty; perhaps I really did have a secret desire for my father’s ... death, but I swear I was not as guilty as you think, and perhaps I didn’t urge you on at all. No, no, I didn’t urge you on! But no matter, I will give evidence against myself tomorrow at the trial. I’m determined to! I’ll tell everything, everything. But we’ll appear together. And whatever you say against me at the trial, whatever evidence you give, I’ll face it; I’m not afraid of you. I’ll confirm it all myself! But you must confess too! You must, you must; we’ll go together. That’s how it will be!”
Ivan said this solemnly and resolutely, and from his flashing eyes alone it could be seen that it would be so.
“You’re ill, I see; you’re quite ill. Your eyes are yellow,” Smerdyakov remarked, without the least irony, with apparent sympathy in fact.
“We’ll go together,” Ivan repeated. “And if you won’t go, no matter, I’ll go alone.”
Smerdyakov paused as though thinking it over.
“Nothing of the sort will happen, and you won’t go,” he concluded at last, firmly.
“You don’t understand me,” Ivan exclaimed reproachfully.

“You’ll be too ashamed, if you confess it all. And what’s more, it will be no use at all, because I’ll say straight out that I never said anything of the sort to you, and that you’re either ill (and it looks like it, too), or you’re so sorry for your brother that you’re sacrificing yourself to save him and have invented it all against me, since you’ve never thought any more of me than if I were a fly. And who will believe you, and what single proof have you got?”
“Listen, you showed me those notes just now to convince me.”
Smerdyakov lifted the book off the notes and set it to one side.
“Take that money away with you,” Smerdyakov sighed.
“Of course I’ll take it. But why do you give it to me, if you committed the murder for the sake of it?” Ivan looked at him with great surprise.

“I don’t want it,” Smerdyakov said in a shaking voice, with a gesture of refusal. “I did have an idea of starting a new life with that money in Moscow or, better still, abroad. I did dream of it, mainly because ‘all things are lawful.’ That was quite right, what you taught me, because you talked to me a great deal about it. For if there’s no everlasting God, there’s no such thing as virtue, and no need of it. You were right about that. So that’s how I looked at it.”
“Did you come to that on your own?” asked Ivan, with a wry smile.
“With your guidance.”
“And now, I suppose, you believe in God, since you’re giving back the money?”
“No, I don’t believe,” whispered Smerdyakov.
“Then why are you giving it back?”

“Leave off ... that’s enough!” Smerdyakov waved his hand again. “You used to say yourself that everything was lawful, so why are you so upset now, too? You even want to go and give evidence against yourself.... Only nothing of the sort will happen! You won’t go and give evidence,” Smerdyakov declared with conviction.
“You’ll see,” said Ivan.

“It’s not possible. You’re very clever. You’re fond of money, I know that. You like to be respected, too, because you’re very proud; you’re far too fond of women’s charms, too, and what you mind most of all is living in undisturbed comfort, without having to depend on anyone—that’s what you care about most. You won’t want to spoil your life forever by taking such a disgrace on yourself. You’re like Fyodor Pavlovitch, you’re more like him than any of his children; you have the same soul he had.”
“You’re not a fool,” said Ivan, seeming struck. The blood rushed to his face. “You’re serious now!” he remarked, looking at Smerdyakov suddenly with a different expression.
“It was your pride that made you think I was a fool. Take the money.”
Ivan took the three rolls of notes and put them in his pocket without wrapping them in anything.
“I’ll show them in court tomorrow,” he said.
“Nobody will believe you, since you have plenty of money of your own; you might simply have taken it out of your cash-box and brought it to the court.”
Ivan rose from his seat.
“I repeat,” he said, “the only reason I haven’t killed you is that I need you for tomorrow. Remember that, don’t forget it!”

“Well, kill me. Kill me now,” Smerdyakov said, all at once looking strangely at Ivan. “You won’t even dare do that!” he added with a bitter smile. “You won’t dare do anything, you, who used to be so bold!”
“Till tomorrow,” cried Ivan, and moved to go out.
“Wait a moment.... Show me those notes again.”
Ivan took out the notes and showed them to him. Smerdyakov looked at them for ten seconds.
“Well, you can go,” he said, with a wave of his hand. “Ivan Fyodorovitch!” he called after him again.
“What do you want?” Ivan turned without stopping.
“Good-bye!”
“Till tomorrow!” Ivan cried again, and he walked out of the cottage.

The snowstorm was still raging. He walked the first few steps boldly, but suddenly began to stagger. “It’s something physical,” he thought with a grin. Something like joy was rising in his heart. He felt an unbounded resolution; he would put an end to the wavering that had tortured him so lately. His mind was made up, “and now it won’t change,” he thought with relief. At that moment he stumbled against something and almost fell. Stopping short, he made out at his feet the peasant he had knocked down, still lying senseless and motionless. The snow had almost covered his face. Ivan seized him and lifted him in his arms. He saw a light in the little house to the right, went up, knocked at the shutters, and asked the owner of the house to help him carry the peasant to the police station, promising him three roubles. The man got ready and came out. I won’t describe in detail how Ivan managed it, bringing the peasant to the police station and arranging for a doctor to see him at once, and paying generously for the expenses. I will only say that this business took a whole hour, but Ivan was well content with it. His mind wandered and worked without stopping.

“If I hadn’t made my decision so firmly for tomorrow,” he reflected with satisfaction, “I wouldn’t have stayed a whole hour to look after the peasant, but would have walked past, without caring whether he froze. I’m quite capable of watching myself, by the way,” he thought at the same instant, with still greater satisfaction, “although they’ve decided that I’m going out of my mind!”

Just as he reached his own house he stopped short, suddenly asking himself whether he had better go at once to the prosecutor and tell him everything. He settled the question by turning back to the house. “Everything together tomorrow!” he whispered to himself, and, strange to say, almost all his gladness and self-satisfaction vanished in an instant.

As he entered his own room, he felt something like a touch of ice on his heart, like a memory or, more exactly, a reminder, of something agonizing and revolting that was in that room now, at that moment, and had been there before. He sank wearily onto his sofa. The old woman brought him a samovar; he made tea, but did not touch it. He sat on the sofa and felt dizzy. He felt that he was ill and helpless. He began to drop off to sleep, but got up uneasily and walked across the room to shake off his drowsiness. At moments he thought he was delirious, but it was not illness that he thought about most. Sitting down again, he began looking round, as though searching for something. This happened several times. At last his eyes fixed intently on one point. Ivan smiled, but an angry flush spread over his face. He sat a long time in his place with his head propped on both arms, though he kept looking sideways at the same point, at the sofa that stood against the opposite wall. There was clearly something there, some object, that irritated him, worried him and tormented him.
